newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Commission seeks to tackle EU environment law breaches.
newsitem.headline: Commission seeks to tackle EU environment law breaches.

text.p: The European Commission is due to adopt a communication on Tuesday on member states' implementation of environmental law, part of plans to improve compliance across the Union.

The text is due to pass as an "A" point at Tuesday's Commission meeting in Strasbourg, that is to say without discussion, with the recent weekly heads-of-cabinet meeting having waved it through with minimal changes.
At the communication's heart is a three-point plan to improve member states' poor record on implementation of EU environmental legislation.
"This is not a 'which is good, which is bad' exercise. There is a problem: too many cases are pending before the court," one Commission official said.

Last year the Commission clocked 265 reported breaches of EU environmental law, a figure representing 20 percent of all the breaches notified to the Commission. At any one time, the Commission said it has 600 environmental infringement cases outstanding with member states.
Commission figures for July 1996 showed that there were 85 such cases pending before the European Court of Justice.
The communication suggests the problem requires "more radical changes" than could be achieved through alterations to practices and procedures under The Treaty's Article 169.

It is to present three ideas for discussion, namely suggested guidelines for member states to set up inspection systems where they do not already exist, an examination of member states' procedures for dealing with and investigating complaints, and a look at the legal possibilities for environmental organisations to pursue complaints against suspected law-breakers.
"It is a communication. In the light of reactions in the European Parliament and the Council the Commission will consider what measures it might propose," the official said.
